title: The U.K. Is Falling for Palantir’s Salesmanship
gist: The author argues Palantir has won hundreds of millions in U.K. contracts—including a 240 million pound deal and the NHS Federated Data Platform—through military-aesthetic 'theater' and a 'land and expand' lock-in model, despite the products being ordinary and often ineffective (52 of 139 'live' NHS trusts used no app; contested performance claims), while European peers like France exit over digital sovereignty.

insights.claim: In February 2025, then-UK PM Keir Starmer visited Palantir's showroom in a meeting arranged by then-ambassador Peter Mandelson, whose lobbying firm Global Counsel counted Palantir as a client worth more than 30,000 pounds a month, and Palantir was awarded a 240 million pound ($327.1 million) contract shortly after.
insights.speaker: Gareth Watkins
insights.so_what: Documents the lobbying-to-contract pipeline behind Palantir's UK revenue, a governance/conflict-of-interest signal for investors weighing the durability of its public-sector bookings.
insights.quote: the 240 million pound ($327.1 million) contract that Palantir was awarded shortly afterward
insights.locator: In February 2025, then-U.K. Prime Minister Keir Starmer

insights.claim: Palantir places a military and intelligence aesthetic front and center—dark 'tactical' interfaces, blacked-out London offices with NDAs to enter, and systems like TITAN—as marketing 'theater' rather than reflecting the ordinary reality of data visualization.
insights.speaker: Gareth Watkins
insights.so_what: Frames Palantir's brand premium as aesthetic persuasion over product substance—relevant to whether its valuation rests on capability or narrative.
insights.quote: It’s theater, and so is the product.

themes.theme: The NHS deployment and lock-in model

insights.claim: Palantir entered the NHS during the pandemic for 1 pound over four months, then won the contract to build the NHS Federated Data Platform, but 52 of the 139 'live' trusts used no Federated Data Platform app in the year before June, with internal briefings calling the interface 'slow and clunky.'
insights.speaker: Gareth Watkins
insights.so_what: Low real-world adoption despite a flagship contract suggests Palantir's public-sector revenue may not reflect delivered value, a due-diligence red flag.
insights.quote: 52 of the 139 trusts that the NHS classifies as “live” did not use a single Federated Data Platform app in the year preceding this June
insights.locator: That foothold became a much larger contract

insights.claim: Foxglove's Donald Campbell describes Palantir's model as 'land and expand'—arriving cheap or free, learning the system, then making itself hard to remove—creating vendor lock-in because customers 'don't really own what you're building'; the UK Defense Ministry conceded a supplier change would mean rebuilding the architecture from scratch.
insights.speaker: Gareth Watkins
insights.so_what: The proprietary lock-in is Palantir's real moat and revenue-retention mechanism—but also its regulatory and reputational vulnerability if governments push back.
insights.quote: It’s a subscription service with a huge risk of lock-in, because you don’t really own what you’re building.
insights.locator: Donald Campbell, the director of advocacy at Foxglove

insights.claim: Palantir and ministers repeatedly cited that its software delivered 110,000 additional NHS operations, but a quietly added methodology note concedes the analysis 'can't establish cause and effect,' and the UK Statistics Authority warned NHS England over its use of statistics to promote the platform.
insights.speaker: Gareth Watkins
insights.so_what: A headline ROI figure that fails under scrutiny undermines the evidentiary basis for Palantir contracts and invites regulatory/political challenge.
insights.quote: even by NHS England’s own admission, very quietly, the claim doesn’t stand up at all
insights.locator: Palantir and ministers have leaned on a single number

insights.claim: France's internal security service dropped Palantir this year for domestic firm ChapsVision, citing digital sovereignty as Germany and Spain also have—suggesting the tool is not indispensable—while Palantir's US position is unassailable but its Trump White House intimacy makes it 'toxic almost everywhere else.'
insights.speaker: Gareth Watkins
insights.so_what: European digital-sovereignty exits cap Palantir's international expansion runway and expose concentration risk in its US/UK footprint.
insights.quote: its intimacy with the Trump White House and, frankly, extremely odd executive team make it toxic almost everywhere else
insights.locator: Other governments haven’t been so willing

insights.claim: Peter Thiel's Zero to One holds that 'competition is for losers' and 'monopoly is the condition of every successful business,' and Thiel calls Britain's affection for the NHS 'Stockholm syndrome,' while Alex Karp's The Technological Republic argues tech has 'feminized' the West and urges a return to 'hard' weapons engineering.
insights.speaker: Gareth Watkins
insights.so_what: The founders' explicitly monopoly-and-national-purpose ideology explains Palantir's lock-in strategy and defense pivot—useful for anticipating its product and political direction.

insights.claim: The author contends British leaders buy Palantir because they govern with depleted state capacity—citing HS2 shrinking to a London-Birmingham stub with costs rising from 33 billion to as much as 100 billion pounds, and G4S failing to staff the 2012 Olympics, forcing 3,500 soldiers to fill in.
insights.speaker: Gareth Watkins
insights.so_what: Frames Palantir's demand as a symptom of hollowed-out state capacity—implying its public-sector market is driven by institutional weakness rather than product merit.
insights.quote: gained power only to discover that it is the power to administer decline
insights.locator: Consider the circumstances of the British leaders
